label: Grasping and Manipulation
notes: This chapter studies what a contact can prevent, permit, or command when a robot touches an object. Across printed pages 461 to 512 we treat each contact as a geometric constraint on motion and a generator of admissible force, then ask when contacts together immobilize a grasped part securely.

label: The Chapter Question
notes: The unifying thread is to separate what a contact says about motion from what it says about force. Rolling, sliding, and breaking are motion modes; friction cones and wrench cones are force objects. Closure asks whether contacts together span every motion or every wrench the world might demand of the grasp.

label: Contact Kinematics
notes: A nonadhesive point contact forbids interpenetration along the normal but may open if bodies separate. The first-order condition signs the normal component of relative velocity, classifying each contact instant as rolling, sliding, or breaking. These local rules decide which relative twists between hand and object are kinematically admissible at that instant.

label: Roll-Slide-Break Conditions
notes: Let the contact normal point into the object. The signed normal speed of approach determines the mode: zero with matched tangents means rolling, zero with relative tangential motion means sliding, and positive separation means the contact breaks. Penetration, a negative value, is physically forbidden by the unilateral nonpenetration constraint at the point.

label: The Coulomb Friction Cone
notes: Coulomb friction bounds the tangential force by the coefficient times the normal force, so admissible contact forces fill a cone about the surface normal. The half-angle is the friction angle, the arctangent of the coefficient. Any force inside the cone sticks; a force on the boundary is on the verge of sliding.

label: Linearized Friction Cone
notes: The curved friction cone is awkward for linear algebra, so we replace it with a polyhedral inner approximation: a finite fan of edge rays whose nonnegative span lies inside the true cone. More rays approximate the cone better. This conversion turns force-closure questions into linear feasibility checks and small linear programs.

label: Contact Wrench Cone
notes: Each admissible contact force at a point produces a wrench on the object, a moment paired with a force. Mapping every ray of the friction cone through this point gives the contact wrench cone, the set of wrenches one contact can transmit. The grasp combines these cones additively in wrench space across all contacts.

label: The Grasp Map
notes: The grasp map collects each contact's wrench generators as columns acting on contact-force coordinates. In the plane a force at a point contributes a moment equal to the cross product plus the two force components. The image of this map is exactly the set of wrenches the grasp can apply to the object.

label: Form Closure
notes: Form closure immobilizes an object with frictionless contacts alone: the contact normals must positively span the wrench space so that no infinitesimal twist escapes. In the plane first-order form closure needs at least four contacts, in space at least seven. Geometry alone, not friction, blocks every motion here.

label: Force Closure
notes: Force closure allows friction, so the contact wrench cones, not just the normals, must positively span every wrench direction. With friction far fewer contacts suffice: two soft-finger or three point contacts can secure a planar object. Force closure means the grasp can resist any external disturbance wrench applied to the part.

label: A Grasp That Fails
notes: Three contacts pushing symmetrically through a disk's center balance forces but generate no torque about the center, so the grasp map has rank two, not three. The picture looks secure while the algebra exposes a missing wrench direction. Offsetting a contact or adding friction tangents restores the torque authority.

label: Manipulation Modes
notes: Beyond static holding, contacts let a robot push, pivot, and topple parts using controlled sliding and tipping about an edge. The same friction-cone and wrench reasoning predicts whether a pushed object rotates which way or whether it tips. Closure is the secure limit; manipulation deliberately uses the unsecure contact modes to advantage.

label: Recap and Synthesis
notes: Contacts are dual objects: constraints on motion and generators of force. Friction cones make unilateral contact geometric, wrench cones lift that to the object, and closure becomes a positive-spanning test in wrench space. Read the contact picture and the grasp-map rank together, never as two separate facts about the grasp.
